headlines.article_text: Nvidia, SK Hynix, ASML, SoftBank stocks: Global tech rout, AI funding worries Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia, Micron and AMD dropped in premarket trading on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued a plummet. 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion so far this week. The declines came as investors grew increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending In this article 9984.T-JP TSM ASM-NL NVDA SKHY ASML CRWV INTC NOK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Nvidia , Micron and AMD were all down in premarket trading on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued a plummet that's seen over $1 trillion wiped from their market caps this week. Nvidia fell 1.8%, Micron 4.2%, AMD 3.1%. Neoclouds also dropped, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius 4%. Oracle was trading at 1.6% lower. 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment. A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday. South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%. In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC , the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%. Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML was last down 5.2%, Infineon Technologies shed 8.2% and ASM International was down 8.6%. Why are stocks selling off? The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom. Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028." Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity. The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%. watch now VIDEO 6:59 06:59 Kospi on track for weakest close since April as global AI sell-off deepens Squawk Box Europe Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust. "Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note. The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs. "What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs. headlines.summary: SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron have been some of the hardest-hit names in the latest tech sell-off.
headlines.article_text: Memory stocks get hit. China and oversupply are the big worries Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron have been some of the hardest-hit names in the recent tech sell-off. Investor concern over competition from China's CXMT and potential oversupply of memory chips has created headwinds for memory stocks. A column in a South Korean business newspaper suggested oversupply of memory in 2029 added to pressure on the market. In this article SKHY MU Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Korea KOSPI Index displayed on a smartphone with SK hynix and Samsung logo displayed. Cfoto | Future Publishing | Getty Images Memory chip stocks have taken a particularly bad beating this week amid broader equity market turmoil. Two concerns are adding to the pressure — the debate over whether Chinese competition is threatening memory incumbents and speculation about when the market could become oversupplied. Over the last five days, SK Hynix has plunged 26%, Samsung has tanked 22% and Micron has dropped around 11%. China worries The initial jitters came at the start of the week after China's leading memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , announced plans to roll out a server memory product based on new architecture . CXMT's design would allow higher storage density, raising concerns that the breakthrough could result in the Chinese company taking global market share from rivals Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. However, a number of analysts questioned whether CXMT would be able to scale the production of such an advanced technology. watch now VIDEO 6:59 06:59 Kospi on track for weakest close since April as global AI sell-off deepens Squawk Box Europe "The issue, of course, was with any architectural change ... you can make the chips, but what yield are you getting? If you're only getting a 50% yield, you're literally putting half the chips in the bin because they don't work very well," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday. Kevin Cassidy, a senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, also said the developments at CXMT are unlikely to add more supply of memory onto the market. "We don't think this is going to swing the supply-demand equation at all," Cassidy told CNBC. Oversupply by 2029? Traders are also discussing comments from an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper , a prominent South Korean publication, in which a reporter urged the country's government to prepare for a slowdown in the AI boom and to identify and develop the next big growth engine. The writer said that two people — Professor Hwang of the Seoul National University and Ahn Ki-hyun, executive director of the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association — expect to see a "flood of new supply" that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" in 2029, according to a CNBC translation. By 2030, "the supercycle could be over and the industry could enter a downturn," the writer said. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded to the article in a post on X , saying that China "will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028." watch now VIDEO 5:07 05:07 Rosenblatt's Kevin Cassidy on CXMT's new memory design: Don't think it will swing supply-demand equation Squawk Box Random access memory (RAM) is produced by the likes of SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron as well as CXMT in China. An oversupply of RAM in 2029 would pose yet another headwind for memory stocks, with lower prices and a squeeze on profit margins. But a forecast that far out hasn't been echoed by other analysts. Typically, the biggest customers for memory chips have been consumer electronics companies, because memory is a key component of devices like smartphones and laptops. But with the AI boom picking up pace, memory has also become a key component of Nvidia chips and other parts of the data center supply chain. With demand increasing, supply has tightened, leading to unprecedented price rises. That has led to huge rallies in the share price of Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the three biggest memory makers. But a key question for investors is whether the industry’s typical boom-and-bust cycle is finally changing. Memory prices have traditionally surged when demand outstrips supply, only to fall as manufacturers ramp up production and the market becomes oversupplied. Investors are trying to work out if that cycle no longer exists or whether there has been a fundamental change. All of the major memory makers are currently in the process of expanding capacity, but it takes around three to five years for a factory to be built and come online. That has led many analysts to forecast that the shortage won't ease until 2028 — but that might not necessarily lead to huge price declines. Counterpoint Research sees the price of DRAM, another key type of memory, falling around 23% in 2028 compared with 2027. However, the DRAM price would still be up around 230% compared to 2025. "The current memory market is considered to be in a 'New Normal' era, and the down cycle will differ from previous ones," Jeongku Choi, senior research analyst at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC. "Suppliers and buyers enter into 3- to 5-year Long-Term Agreements (LTAs), involving substantial upfront payments and established upper and lower price limits to ensure consistency. Consequently, even if a down cycle occurs, it is not expected to show the same sharp decline seen in the past." — CNBC's Lisa Kim helped contribute to this report. Amazon Amazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market. The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor. Amazon acquired Bee , a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations. The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post. Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said. Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware . Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets , while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia -powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI. The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market. The $100 Bee Eclipse is a credit card-sized device that magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. Meta has seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers. Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called Muse Charm that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. Plaud developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and Friend offers an AI necklace. Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word. When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions. With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said. An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said. headlines.article_text: What is Starshield? SpaceX's military Starlink explained Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Starshield is SpaceX's government-focused satellite network, and new restrictions reported by Ukraine have renewed scrutiny of how it differs from the company's commercial Starlink service. It is a secure satellite network for government and national security users, built using Starlink technology and SpaceX launch capabilities. The service adds government-focused security, dedicated user equipment, and missions such as Earth observation and hosted payloads. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Uncertainty over who controls SpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention, as restrictions on the technology hinder Ukraine's defenses. Ukraine has accused SpaceX -owned Starlink of restricting its military-grade services , known as Starshield, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv. Officials in Kyiv said SpaceX had imposed restrictions on Starshield without advance notice, disrupting military operations and hampering efforts to protect civilians amid intense Russian attacks this week. In response, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk appeared to shift responsibility for any changes to Starshield's use in Ukraine to the U.S. government and President Donald Trump . He said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by Washington, with the U.S. military and ultimately the president determining any limits on their use. The White House and the Pentagon didn't immediately reply to CNBC's request for comment. Here's what to know about Starshield, and how it differs from Starlink. What is Starshield and how does it work? Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network designed for government and national security use, building on the technology developed for Starlink.
